deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT (p.94). The problem is the general reversion of series. Given p^m = Q(q) = q^n + a q^{n+nu} + b q^{n+2nu} + ..., express q^theta as a series in p. On p.94 Gauss sets x = q^nu, f(x) = (1 + a x + b x^2 + ...)^{-nu/n} and u = p^{nu m/n}, so that x = u f(x). He applies Lagrange's theorem to x = t + u f(x). He writes the coefficient of u^k in coefficient-extraction ('Coeff') form, replaces the dummy variable t by q^nu, uses f(q^nu) = q^nu Q^{-nu/n}, and puts lambda = theta/nu.

THIS PAGE.

(1) Substitution. Putting u^{(theta+j nu)/nu} = p^{(theta+j nu)m/n} into the last line of p.94 gives
 q^theta = sum_{j>=0} theta/(theta+j nu) * p^{(theta+j nu)m/n} * [q^{-theta}] Q^{-(theta+j nu)/n}.
This is the first display (terms j = 0, 1, 2, etc.).

(2) Uniform coefficient formula. Write P := q^theta, viewed as a function of p, and mu := (theta+j nu)m/n. Then theta/(theta+j nu) = theta m/(mu n) and Q^{-(theta+j nu)/n} = Q^{-mu/m}. Hence
 [p^mu] P = (theta m)/(mu n) * [q^{-theta}] Q^{-mu/m}.
In modern terms: put z = p^{m/n}, g(q) = Q^{1/n} = q(1+...)^{1/n}, so z = g(q). The Lagrange-Buermann formula [z^k] q^theta = (theta/k)[q^{-theta}] g^{-k} with k = n mu/m gives exactly this.

(3) Generating-function (constant-term) form. Differentiate: dP/dp = sum_mu mu c_mu p^{mu-1} = (theta m/n) sum_j p^{mu-1} [q^{-theta}] Q^{-mu/m}. This equals the q-free term of
 m theta (p^m/Q)^{theta/n} q^theta / ( n p (1 - (p^m/Q)^{nu/n}) ).
To see this (my step), expand the geometric series sum_j (p^m/Q)^{(theta+j nu)/n}. Each term contributes (m theta/(n p)) p^mu q^theta Q^{-mu/m}, whose q^0 coefficient is the required one. The expansion is understood formally: first in powers of p, then term-by-term in Laurent series in q.

(4) Proposed generalisation. Let P(p) = Q(q), with Q of the same lacunary form. Let 𝔓(P) be the expansion of an arbitrary f(q). Gauss asserts
 d𝔓/dP = constant term ('pars absoluta sive a q libera') of q f'(q) (P/Q)^{1/n} / ( n P (1 - (P/Q)^{nu/n}) ).
For f = q^theta and P = p^m this is consistent with (3): q f' = theta q^theta, and the chain-rule factor d(p^m)/dp = m p^{m-1} reconciles the two. But see errors: the factor (P/Q)^{1/n} is the theta = 1 case.

(5) Derivation of Lagrange's theorem itself ('s. u. S. 273' is a cross-reference). From x = t + u f(x), implicit differentiation gives (my steps)
 dx/du = f/(1 - u f'), dx/dt = 1/(1 - u f'),
hence dx/du = f(x) dx/dt.
- More generally, suppose F_1'(x) = f(x) F'(x), i.e. dF_1 x = f x dFx. Then dF/du = F' f dx/dt = F_1' dx/dt = dF_1/dt.
- Iterate along a chain F, F_1, F_2, ... with F_{k}' = f F_{k-1}'. Since d/du and d/dt commute, d^2F/du^2 = d/dt(dF_1/du) = d^2F_2/dt^2, and in general d^kF/du^k = d^kF_k/dt^k.
- (Implicit continuation, mine) At u = 0, x = t, and d^kF_k/dt^k = d^{k-1}/dt^{k-1}[f(t)^k F'(t)]. Taylor expansion in u then gives Lagrange's series F(x) = F(t) + sum u^k/k! d^{k-1}/dt^{k-1}[f^k F'].
This is Laplace's classical proof.
errors: Step (4), the general formula with the factor (P/Q)^{1/n}/(1-(P/Q)^{nu/n}), is obtained from (3) by replacing theta by 1. It is correct only when f(q) contains only powers q^{1+j nu} (exponents congruent to 1 mod nu). For a general power series f one needs the sum over all k>=1: (P/Q)^{1/n}/(1-(P/Q)^{1/n}). More precisely, it needs the sum over all k congruent to the exponents of f mod nu. Counterexample: n=nu=2, Q=q^2+a q^4, P=s, f=q^2. As written the formula gives d𝔓/ds = 0, whereas the true value is 1/sqrt(1+4as) = 1 - 2as + ... . With denominator 1-(P/Q)^{1/2} it gives the correct value.

In (3) the 'q-free term' must be taken after expanding first in powers of p (geometric series), then each term as a Laurent series in q. Done naively in q alone the expression is not a well-defined Laurent series. This is tacit but harmless.
Bottom derivation: the stray marks in 'dx/du' and 'dF_1x/dt' are crossings-out, not content. The steps are correct, including the tacit interchange of d/du and d/dt.
Upstream (p.94, not this page): the series written there for 'fx^lambda' with derivatives of ft^{lambda+k} is notationally confused; the final Coeff-form used on this page is nevertheless correct.

results.what: Coefficient formula for reversion of p^m = q^n + a q^{n+nu} + ...: [p^mu] q^theta = (theta m)/(mu n) [q^{-theta}] Q^{-mu/m}
results.modern_name: Lagrange-Buermann inversion formula in coefficient (residue) form
results.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1770), Buermann (1799); residue/coefficient form often attributed to Jacobi (1830)

results.what: dP/dp equals the q-free (constant) term of m theta (p^m/Q)^{theta/n} q^theta / (n p (1-(p^m/Q)^{nu/n}))
results.modern_name: Constant-term / generating-function form of Lagrange inversion (summing the Lagrange coefficients into a geometric series)
results.usually_credited_to: Variants appear in Jacobi (1830) and later in Good (1960)-type constant-term formulations

results.what: Generalisation to arbitrary f(q) under P(p)=Q(q), stated as a constant-term formula for d𝔓/dP
results.modern_name: Lagrange-Buermann for general analytic function, constant-term form

results.what: Proof of Lagrange's series: x = t + u f(x) implies dx/du = f(x) dx/dt, and d^kF/du^k = d^kF_k/dt^k with F_k' = f F_{k-1}'
results.modern_name: Laplace's proof of the Lagrange inversion theorem

deep.surprise_reason: Lagrange inversion was standard by 1809, and Gauss used it in Theoria motus (Kepler's equation); the Laplace-style proof is textbook. The only mildly non-standard element is packaging the inversion coefficients into a constant-term formula with a geometric-series kernel, anticipating Jacobi's 1830 residue formulation. Even this is a modest reformulation, and Gauss's general version contains a restriction/slip.

checkable.asserts: Test case m=n=nu=theta=1, Q=q+a q^2: the true reversion coefficients.
